title: Tataka
hook: Rama decides, and tries the gentlest way first

segments.voice: Yesterday: a forest that used to be farmland, a yakshi under a curse, and Rama's real question. Your line was Rama stops and asks.

Rama has listened, and his answer isn't a simple yes. My father told me to do whatever you say, he tells the sage. So I'll do this, for the sake of the cows, the sages and the land. He's acting from obedience, from a promise, not from appetite for a fight. Then he lifts his bow and twangs the string. The sound rolls through the forest. And from deep in the trees, something hears it and comes running.
screen: `MY FATHER TOLD ME TO OBEY YOU.` → `THE TWANG OF THE BOWSTRING.` → `SOMETHING COMES RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Tataka charges out, raising clouds of dust, hurling rocks. Valmiki slows down here. Rama doesn't try to kill her. I'll just take away her power to harm, he tells Lakshmana; I don't want to take her life. He shoots and cuts off her arms. Lakshmana wounds her face. That should end it. It doesn't. Tataka uses her magic, turns invisible, changes shape, and rains stones on them from the air. Enough mercy, Rama, Vishvamitra calls. Evening is coming, and at dusk rakshasas grow stronger. So Rama, tracking her by sound, looses an arrow, and Tataka falls. The gods appear and praise Rama, Vishvamitra embraces him and kisses his head, and the forest, the text says, is freed and becomes beautiful again. How do people read this scene? Traditional teachers see Rama's first act of protection, a land given back to the people meant to live in it, and they point to how hard he tried not to kill. Some modern readers find it painful, a young man pressed to kill a woman, and read the story with that discomfort in view. Both readings take the text seriously. What the text itself makes plain is the order of things. He asked first. He obeyed a promise. He tried to disarm before he destroyed. Only when that failed did he finish it.
screen: `HE TRIES TO DISARM, NOT KILL.` · `SHE TURNS INVISIBLE, RAINS STONES.` · `AT DUSK, THE FINAL ARROW.` · `TWO WAYS PEOPLE READ IT.` · then, large: `THE FOREST IS FREED.`

segments.voice: Think of a situation where you had to be firm with someone, or will have to, and hold one question with the breath: what's the gentlest thing that would actually work? Don't plan the whole conversation; let the gentlest step come into view, and rest with it.
Tataka. Rama, obeying his father's word, first tries to disarm her, and only when her magic goes on does he loose the arrow that frees the forest.
Your line: disarm before he destroyed. Force came last, not first. That's day five hundred one.

howItsDone: In Ramayana recitation and performance, Tataka's defeat is told as Rama's first act of protecting the land; commentators and modern readers discuss it in different ways, and some draw attention to Rama's reluctance.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 26 gives Rama's stated reason, his father's command, and his wish not to kill; Lakshmana's wounding of her face mirrors a later scene with Shurpanakha in the Aranya Kanda.

chat.says: In Valmiki's telling, did Rama set out to kill Tataka right away?
options: No. He tried only to disarm her first, and loosed the last arrow when that failed.
No. He refused to fight her, and Lakshmana ended it while Rama watched.
No. He talked her into leaving, and she fled the forest for good that day.
chat.meaning: Rama told Lakshmana he only wanted to take away her power to harm. Only when her magic went on did he loose the final arrow.

Tataka.meaning: the yakshi who turned two rich lands into wilderness

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, always at his side

rakshasas.meaning: demon beings of the epic, said to grow stronger at dusk

Valmiki.meaning: the poet-sage credited with the Ramayana

Vishvamitra.meaning: the king-turned-sage leading the two princes

recall: the old bear who reminds Hanuman
